analysis.one_liner: Replaces private health insurance with a government-run program covering everyone with no copays or deductibles.
analysis.headline: The bill, which had 88 Democratic cosponsors, was referred to three House committees and never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote before the Congress ended in January 2011.
analysis.plain_summary: H.R. 676 would have replaced Medicare, Medicaid, CHIP, and most private health insurance with a single government-run program covering every U.S. resident. It would have paid for all medically necessary care, including dental, vision, mental health, prescription drugs, and long-term care, with no deductibles, copays, or coinsurance. Funding would come from money already spent on federal health programs plus new taxes on the top 5% of earners, a payroll tax, and a small tax on stock and bond trades. Private insurers would have been barred from selling coverage that duplicates the program, and investor-owned hospitals would have had to convert to nonprofit status.
analysis.who_benefits: Every U.S. resident, who would get free coverage for all medically necessary care with no premiums or out-of-pocket costs; displaced insurance-billing workers would get first priority in retraining and two years of salary-parity transition benefits.

how_it_helps.text: All individuals residing in the U.S. and its territories are covered and receive a national health insurance card, with coverage for primary care, hospital care, prescription drugs, long-term care, mental health, dental, vision, and hearing services [S2].
No deductibles, copayments, coinsurance, or other cost-sharing may be imposed on covered benefits [S3].

Funding combines existing federal health revenues with higher income taxes on the top 5% of earners, a progressive payroll and self-employment excise tax, and a small tax on stock and bond transactions [S2].

Insurance-company, hospital, and office clerical and billing workers whose jobs are eliminated get first priority in retraining and up to two years of transition benefits equal to their prior salary, capped at $100,000 per year [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The top 5% of income earners, through higher income taxes; all workers, through a payroll excise tax; investors, through a tax on stock and bond trades; and private insurers and investor-owned hospitals, whose core business is eliminated.

drawbacks.text: The program is funded by raising personal income taxes on the top 5% of earners, a progressive payroll and self-employment excise tax, and a small tax on stock and bond transactions [S2].
Private health insurers would be barred from selling any coverage duplicating the program's benefits, leaving them only supplemental products like cosmetic-surgery coverage [S2].

Institutions could only participate if public or not-for-profit; investor-owned hospitals choosing to participate would be required to convert to nonprofit status, with owners compensated for financial losses over 15 years through Treasury bond sales [S3].

Hospital payments would shift to annually negotiated global budgets set by program directors, and physician pay to a negotiated national fee schedule, giving government administrators substantial control over provider revenue [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would guarantee free, comprehensive coverage to every resident and eliminate premiums, deductibles, and billing paperwork, at the cost of significant new taxes concentrated on high earners, payroll, and financial trades. It would erase the private insurance industry's main product and force for-profit hospitals to convert. The honest objection is not only the taxes but the concentration of budget-setting power in a federal program: hospital global budgets and a national fee schedule mean the government's payment levels would directly determine access to care, with no private alternative if funding falls short.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to three House committees on the day it was introduced and sent to a Health subcommittee the next day, but no committee ever acted on it and it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced January 26, 2009, and referred the same day to the Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, and Natural Resources committees [S5].
The next day it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health [S5].
No further action appears in the record; the bill never received a committee vote or a floor vote in the 111th Congress [S5].
It had 88 Democratic cosponsors alongside sponsor Rep. Conyers, all Democrats, with no Republican support [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private health insurers and investor-owned hospitals kept their existing business intact, and the multi-trillion-dollar insurance and billing economy continued uninterrupted; ordinary Americans remained with the pre-ACA system of premiums and cost-sharing until separate legislation passed later in that Congress.

for.name: John Conyers Jr.
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 88 cosponsors, all fellow House Democrats.

against.name: House committee chairs
against.role: Chairs of Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, and Natural Resources
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill after its referral, so it never advanced out of committee.

against.name: Nancy Pelosi
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the House floor for a vote during the 111th Congress.

against.name: Health insurance industry
against.role: Private insurers and their trade associations
against.what_they_did: Opposed single-payer legislation, which would have barred insurers from selling coverage duplicating the government program.

sides.party_line_note: All 89 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats, roughly a third of the 253-member House Democratic caucus, with no Republican support recorded; the bill also failed to advance under Democratic committee chairs and a Democratic Speaker.

industries.note: The bill makes it unlawful for a private insurer to sell coverage duplicating the government program's benefits, reducing insurers to supplemental products like cosmetic surgery coverage. Their core premiums and administration costs would vanish, which is precisely the paperwork and premium burden the program removes from households.

No for-profit institution could be a participating provider; hospitals opting into the program had to convert to nonprofit status, with owners compensated for losses over 15 years. Investor returns in hospital ownership would have been eliminated.

Drug prices would be set through annual program negotiation with bulk procurement, and the formulary would push prescribing toward generics. Insurers today negotiate drug prices separately; a single national buyer would have had far more leverage.

industries.industry: Health insurance billing and administration workers
industries.note: Jobs tied to insurance claims processing would be eliminated as billing collapses into one system, but the bill guarantees these workers first priority in retraining and two years of salary-parity transition benefits up to $100,000 a year.

industries.industry: Nonprofit HMOs delivering care in their own facilities
industries.note: Salaried-staff nonprofit HMOs could keep participating and receive global budgets or capitation, so one corner of organized delivery keeps a paid role inside the new system.
